name: Felix Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name never goes with your answers. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Granite Insurance's claims hub, a big shed of an office on the industrial estate off the bypass. I'm on the fleet team, so my claims are vans and taxis: a delivery van that's reversed into a bollard, a plumber's van broken into overnight. I check the cover, get the repair estimate in, and authorise the garage to start. When a man's van is his whole living, getting him back on the road fast really matters.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Getting there. I'm still bad at judging whether a repair estimate is padded, which is funny, because my dad has run a car repair garage my whole life. Owen, my supervisor, catches the ones I wave through. I started using the AI helper to draft the authorisation letters a couple of months ago, after half the team did. I live alone in a small flat I bought two years ago with a little mortgage, I've got about eight months' costs saved, and I coach the under-twelves football team on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get back to work. A lot of money got burned on hype. People should've listened to the folk who actually do the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means steady. The letter helper saves a bit of typing, and that's it. A man with a smashed van still wants a person to tell him when he's back on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it and ask Owen to teach me how to spot a padded estimate. I'd spend a couple of Saturdays at Dad's garage watching how he prices a job, since he's the best teacher I've got. And I'd overpay the mortgage a bit each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I'd bet on, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad prices repairs. What would he say about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say insurers always try to squeeze garages, and now his son's the one squeezing. He laughs about it. But he's also proud I've got a steady office job with a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's garage, a bit. He's sixty-one, and with fewer petrol cars there's less engine work. That's nothing to do with AI, but I think about who takes it over.

feel: **Calm**; this is the world he'd **bet on**.

fieldNote: Felix's calm comes from a **steady employer**, his own flat and family nearby.

He enjoys the irony of a garage owner's son now **checking garage bills**.

steps.text: Ask Owen to teach him to spot padded repair estimates
Spend Saturdays at Dad's garage learning how he prices jobs
Overpay the flat mortgage a little each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change comes, and you adapt or you get left behind. Firms have every right to bring in new tools, but they should look after loyal staff and bring back proper apprenticeships for the new jobs. I wouldn't want the government stepping in much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the fleet desk shrinks. Checking cover, authorising repairs, writing letters: that's the list you read out. A junior who still misses padded estimates isn't the one they'll keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which tools actually work for the team, then learn them properly, like I did with the letter helper. I'd ask Owen whether the firm needs motor engineers, the people who inspect damaged vehicles in person. And I'd talk to Dad seriously about the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be lying if I said it didn't keep me thinking at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, if insurance doesn't need me, would you take me on and teach me properly. He'd pretend to think about it for a day. Then he'd make me start at seven sweeping the floor, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms have the right to use the tools. Even if it's your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, even if it's my job. Firms have the right to use new tools, but a decent firm looks after the people who've been loyal. I'd remember which kind Granite turned out to be.

say: I'd say change comes, and you **adapt or get left** behind.
Firms should look after **loyal staff** and bring back proper **apprenticeships**.
think: The **fleet desk shrinks**, since checking and authorising are exactly what AI takes.
A junior who misses **padded estimates** isn't the one they'll keep.
do: Learn the **new tools** properly once they've proven themselves.
Ask Owen about becoming a **motor engineer** who inspects vehicles.
Ask his dad to **take him on** at the garage if needed.
feel: **Anxious**, thinking about it at night without panicking.
S1.quote: Firms have the right to use new tools, but a decent firm looks after the people who've been loyal.
fieldNote: Felix defends a firm's **right to automate**, even his own job.
He looks at the **hands-on inspection** side of motor claims first.
His **father's garage** is a ready fallback, though he'd start by sweeping floors.

steps.text: Learn the team's new claims tools once colleagues show they work

Ask his dad about learning the trade at the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast, and I'd blame the big tech firms for rushing it out. But I'd also say moaning won't fix it. People need to get to work on something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My office job is gone within two years; there's no hiding from that. The garage is hands-on, so it's got until around 2031 before robots can fix cars. After that, nobody knows, and Dad's sixty-one, so it might suit him to retire anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Dad's garage straight away as an apprentice, even before Granite lets me go, and start a mechanic's course at the college at nights. I'd keep the flat, because the mortgage is small, and keep my savings for the gap. I'd also put some of my savings into the kit for electric vans at the garage, since that's where the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. Like the ground's gone soft. But having Dad there is a big thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the lads you coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to fix things, not just use them. Twelve-year-olds don't want to hear it. But I'd say it anyway, between drills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd quit before they let you go. Isn't that a risk, giving up a wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and normally I'm not one to jump first. But in two years everyone in my building is looking for hands-on work at the same time. I'd rather be early than in the queue.

fieldNote: Usually cautious, Felix chooses to **jump early** to beat the queue for hands-on work.

He wants the garage to move into **electric vans**, showing practical thinking.

steps.text: Join Dad's garage as an apprentice before Granite lets him go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and anyone sensible will use it. I'd say firms and colleges should set up proper apprenticeships for adults. Government's job is to get out of the way of that and not tie it in red tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk job goes around 2030. That's when Dad's thinking of retiring anyway, which is almost neat. The garage would carry on until robots get good around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Granite for two or three years, save hard and pay down the mortgage. Meanwhile I'd do the mechanic's qualification part-time and spend Saturdays at the garage. Around 2029 I'd go full-time with Dad and take it over when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels manageable. Five years and a plan beats panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your football coaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it. Saturdays would be the garage in the morning and the under-twelves in the afternoon. My mum says I'll fall over by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2034, when robots come for garage work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be thirty-four, owning a garage with a name people know. Maybe I'd own the robots instead of competing with them. I can't see that far, but owning my dad's garage is better than working for someone else when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse to sit around. Learn a trade, back your family, and let businesses get on with it. That's what I'd say down the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be 37, with the garage probably mine by then. Hands-on work gets until about 2039. I think I'd be all right, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Granite a good few years, get properly good at the job and maybe move up. I'd do the mechanic's qualification slowly, at my own pace. Somewhere around 2031 I'd take over from Dad, and I'd use the AI tools for the garage paperwork once they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a decade, and I've got a trade waiting in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the garage look like in 2035, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four bays, two of them for electric vans. I'd have a computer doing all the quotes and parts orders, so I'm not up till ten doing paperwork like Dad is. My name over the door next to his; that's the dream, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that Dad might not last that long working, because his back's bad. If he stopped early, I'd have to move faster than I'd like. But that's a family thing, not a robot thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because everyone in my building would be fighting for the same hands-on jobs at once. What would help is proper adult apprenticeships, run by firms and colleges, and maybe some help for small businesses like Dad's to take on trainees. I'd rather earn than be handed money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. A lot of us have a dad or an uncle with a garage or a shop, and that's the real safety net round here. If those go under, then people really are stuck.

headlineQuote: A lot of us have a dad or an uncle with a garage or a shop, and that's the real safety net round here.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old fleet claims clerk** at a big insurer, still missing padded estimates.
He owns a **small flat**, has eight months saved, and coaches **under-twelves football**.
Traditional and steady, he backs a firm's **right to automate** but expects loyalty in return.
His fallback in every picture is his **dad's car garage**, hands-on work that buys time.
His mood runs from **calm** to **alarmed**, and back to calm with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because everyone in his office would chase hands-on jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: Proper **adult apprenticeships** run by firms and colleges.
Help for **small family businesses** to take on trainees.
